note: AI futures region, expansion (D-31.18): approved voices and deepening works. Texts are local and never redistributed.

people.name: Zvi Mowshowitz
people.reason: Writes the most-read weekly AI digest in the safety scene and reviews every major model and policy fight in long detail.
people.gap: The map has Yudkowsky and Scott Alexander but no weekly 'working doomer' voice who engages each release and each accelerationist argument point by point.

people.name: Helen Toner
people.reason: Former OpenAI board member and CSET director; writes plainly on timelines, steerability and the 'dynamism vs safety' framing.
people.gap: No governance researcher in the map bridges safety worries with a dynamist, anti-stasis framing.

people.name: Leopold Aschenbrenner
people.reason: 'Situational Awareness' set the 'AGI by 2027, race with China, lock down the labs' frame many on X now use.
people.gap: The map lacks the national-security 'Manhattan Project' view of AGI that sits between safety and e/acc.

people.name: Yoshua Bengio
people.reason: Turing Award winner, chair of the International AI Safety Report and founder of LawZero; the most-cited scientist arguing for catastrophic-risk caution.
people.gap: Safety is voiced by essayists and lab leaders; no top academic ML researcher speaks for it.

people.name: Geoffrey Hinton
people.reason: Nobel laureate who left Google to warn about AI takeover risk; his public voice moved mainstream opinion.
people.gap: Same gap as Bengio; his 'digital intelligence will surpass us' argument is not in the map.

people.name: Holly Elmore
people.reason: Leads PauseAI US; argues the safety movement should campaign publicly for a pause instead of working inside labs.
people.gap: The map has no voice for grassroots pause activism, or for criticism of EA from within the safety camp.
people.flag: Several recent posts attack Anthropic by name (e.g. 'Anthropic delenda est'). That is not a conflict of interest, but the model that built this list is Anthropic's, so Benjamin may want an outside check that her views are summarised fairly.

people.name: Jack Clark
people.reason: Anthropic co-founder and long-time Import AI author; his 'technological optimism and appropriate fear' essay set off the Sacks–Anthropic clash.
people.gap: The map has Dario Amodei but no Anthropic policy voice, and lacks the other side of the Sacks feud.
people.flag: CONFLICT OF INTEREST: Anthropic co-founder and head of policy. Anthropic makes the model that assembled this list. Benjamin to decide.

people.name: Dean W. Ball
people.niche: Right-of-centre AI policy (former White House OSTP adviser)
people.reason: Helped draft the 2025 AI Action Plan and writes Hyperdimensional; a conservative who takes AI capability seriously.
people.gap: The map's right-wing AI voices are Vance, Hawley and Sacks; it lacks a conservative policy writer who is neither populist nor purely accelerationist.

people.name: Samuel Hammond
people.niche: AI policy / state capacity (Foundation for American Innovation)
people.reason: 'Ninety-five theses on AI' and 'AI and Leviathan' argue AGI will remake the state itself; widely read on the tech right.
people.gap: No one in the map covers the 'AI will transform institutions and the state' argument from the right.

people.name: Alondra Nelson
people.reason: Led the Biden White House 'Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights'; argues for a rights-based, democratic approach to AI.
people.gap: The map has no Democratic-administration policy voice on AI.

people.name: Bernie Sanders
people.reason: Senator who frames AI as a war by tech oligarchs on workers and proposes a robot tax, a 32-hour week and slowing AI down.
people.gap: The map has right-populist AI critics (Hawley, Vance) but no left-populist counterpart.

people.name: Divya Siddarth
people.niche: Democratic / collective-intelligence AI governance (Collective Intelligence Project)
people.reason: Co-founded CIP, which runs 'alignment assemblies' and global dialogues to put public input into AI models.
people.gap: Weyl and Tang cover pluralist theory; the map lacks a practitioner of democratic AI governance.
people.flag: CONFLICT CHECK: CIP partnered with Anthropic on 'Collective Constitutional AI' (2023). Her field (deliberative democracy / civic tech) is also Benjamin's own field and may overlap with his network. Benjamin to confirm.

people.name: Demis Hassabis
people.reason: Nobel laureate who heads Google DeepMind; frames AI as a tool for science with 'cautious optimism'.
people.gap: Frontier labs are represented by Altman, Amodei and Musk only; Google DeepMind's science-first view is missing.

people.name: Mustafa Suleyman
people.reason: Head of Microsoft AI; argues against building AI that seems conscious and for 'humanist superintelligence' kept under human control.
people.gap: No lab leader in the map argues against AI personhood or for deliberately bounded superintelligence.

people.name: Mark Zuckerberg
people.reason: Made the business case for open-weight AI, then pivoted to 'personal superintelligence'.
people.gap: The open-source frontier-lab position is absent (Andreessen argues it from outside).

people.name: Yann LeCun
people.reason: Turing Award winner and long-time Meta chief AI scientist; argues LLMs are not the path to human-level AI and that doom talk serves regulatory capture.
people.gap: The map has no top researcher who rejects both the doom case and the 'scaling LLMs is enough' case.

people.name: Meredith Whittaker
people.reason: Argues 'AI' is a product of surveillance capitalism and that agentic AI breaks privacy.
people.gap: Bender, Gebru and Hao cover AI ethics; the political-economy-of-surveillance critique from someone who runs a major tech product is missing.

people.name: Brian Merchant
people.reason: Author of 'Blood in the Machine'; documents AI job losses worker by worker and the growing AI backlash.
people.gap: No labour-side writer documents AI's effect on workers in the map.

people.name: Ed Zitron
people.reason: The loudest voice arguing generative AI is a financial bubble with no sound business model.
people.gap: The 'it's a bubble' economic-sceptic camp is absent.

people.name: Daron Acemoglu
people.reason: Nobel economist who estimates small macro gains from AI and argues for steering AI towards augmenting workers.
people.gap: Cowen and Hanson are the only economists; the map lacks a mainstream academic sceptic of AI-led growth.

people.name: Anton Korinek
people.reason: Models scenarios where AGI makes human labour obsolete and asks what economic policy must do then.
people.gap: No economist in the map takes the full-automation AGI scenario seriously on its own terms.
people.flag: CONFLICT CHECK: reportedly a member of Anthropic's Economic Advisory Council (2025). Not verified in this pass; Benjamin to confirm.

people.name: Pope Leo XIV
people.reason: Chose his name partly because of AI and issued the AI encyclical 'Magnifica Humanitas' (2026).
people.gap: Religious critique is limited to Hawley's covenant framing and Vance's Catholic remarks; the Church's own teaching is not in the map.

people.name: Paul Kingsnorth
people.reason: Orthodox Christian novelist whose essays cast AI as the culmination of a technological civilisation hostile to the human.
people.gap: The map has no anti-modern, spiritual critique of AI.
people.flag: Most of his Substack is paywalled; only the free posts are listed. He is UK/Ireland-based (US-centrality check).

people.name: Arvind Narayanan
people.reason: Princeton computer scientist (with Sayash Kapoor) behind 'AI Snake Oil' and 'AI as Normal Technology', the main rival frame to 'superintelligence soon'.
people.gap: The map has no 'normal technology' voice; Cowen and Hanson are slow-takeoff but not this frame.
people.flag: Most works are co-written with Sayash Kapoor; Benjamin may want to add Kapoor as a joint author or as a second person.

people.name: Gary Marcus
people.reason: Cognitive scientist who argues LLMs cannot reason, AI hype is dangerous, and strong regulation is needed.
people.gap: No 'LLMs are overhyped but still dangerous' voice in the map.

people.name: Andrej Karpathy
people.reason: Former OpenAI and Tesla AI lead whose essays and talks ('Software 2.0', 'animals vs ghosts') shape how builders think about LLMs.
people.gap: The map has no hands-on builder explaining what models are actually like.

people.name: Dwarkesh Patel
people.reason: His podcast is the main long-form venue for lab leaders and researchers, and his essays on timelines are widely debated.
people.gap: No interviewer-essayist from the scene; his 'continual learning is the bottleneck' timelines view is distinctive.

people.name: Venkatesh Rao
people.reason: Long-time TPOT-adjacent essayist who argues against 'hyperanthropomorphism' and for seeing AI as a camera, not an engine.
people.gap: The TPOT scene's own idiom (neither EA nor e/acc) is missing.

people.name: Noah Smith
people.reason: Widely read economics blogger, central on X, who argues AI will leave plenty of good jobs (comparative advantage) and leans optimistic.
people.gap: Techno-optimism in the map comes from VCs (Andreessen, Sacks); there is no economist-blogger making the optimist case.
people.flag: Most recent AI posts are paywalled.
